title: MA9-11186
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXXXXXXX (claimant), a Tamil male, citizen of Sri Lanka, is seeking refugee protection in Canada pursuant to section 96 and section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1.

The claimant alleged that he faced persecution at the hands of the Sri Lankan authorities because he is a Tamil from the north. He alleged a risk of future persecution based on his race, nationality, imputed political opinion and membership in a particular social group if he were to return to Sri Lanka. He also alleged he was accused of being and supporting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE).
The claimant alleged being arrested, detained, beaten and tortured and that his brother suffered the same ill treatment. The claimant's brother fled Sri Lanka in 1998 and now lives in Canada.
The claimant alleged being arrested on XXXX, 2008 in XXXX. He claims he was beaten, threatened and detained for five days.

The claimant left his job on XXXX, 2008 and alleged that he was arrested a second time on XXXX, 2009, put into a white van, taken to a small jail, then beaten and detained for eight days because the police believed that he was helping the LTTE. He was released upon payment of a bribe by his uncle and told to leave XXXX. He went to a private hospital for treatment.

The claimant alleged that his sister XXXX filed a sponsorship application for him but due to the arrest of XXXX, 2009, the claimant fled Sri Lanka without completing the process. The claimant left Sri Lanka on XXXX, 2009 and arrived in the U.S. by route of Russia, Dubai, Cuba, Panama, Haiti and the Dominican Republic on XXXX, 2009. While in the U.S. the claimant filed an asylum claim but withdrew it on XXXX, 2009. He then came to Canada on September 16, 2009.

The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of IRPA, because his narrative was not deemed to be credible. Notwithstanding a nexus to a Convention ground, the Tribunal did not believe that the claimant credibly established that he was being persecuted. Further, the Tribunal found that the claimant was not a Convention refugee due to the fact that there has been a change in circumstances in Sri Lanka and there is no longer an objective basis for his fear. The Tribunal also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection, based on a balance of probabilities, for a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, pursuant to section 97(1)(b) of IRPA. Nor that he would be subject to a danger of torture, pursuant to section 97(1)(a) of IRPA should he return to Sri Lanka.

The determinative issues are credibility, whether there is a personal risk of harm to the claimant today, whether there is a viable internal flight alternative and change in circumstances. ANALYSIS Identity

The Tribunal accepts the photocopies of the claimant's Sri Lankan birth certificate, national ID card and all related documentation seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada. The Tribunal accepts that the claimant is a citizen of Sri Lanka2. Credibility

At the beginning of the hearing the claimant testified that his personal information form (PIF) was true, accurate and up to date. The claimant was an amiable individual whose testimony regarding his allegations was regrettably extremely vague and lacking in sufficient detail or corroborative evidence in support. Though not mandatory, given the allegations presented by the claimant, and the fact that his brother left Sri Lanka a full decade before him, seemingly on similar grounds, the Tribunal found it unfortunate that other than an employment reference letter, the claimant made no efforts to obtain any information to corroborate any aspect of his story.

Although asked repeatedly, the claimant was not able to provide one single document or attestation of proof to support any of his claims. He further failed to demonstrate any systematic persecution over the decade since his brother left Sri Lanka. Nor could he credibly establish what it was that he allegedly suffered during one alleged detention in 2008 or one alleged detention in 2009. Further still, by his own testimony he was allegedly detained on two occasions: once, by the Sri Lankan army allegedly on XXXX, 2008, for five days; and once, by the police six months later, on XXXX, 2009, allegedly for eight days. He was released on both occasions within a reasonably short period of time. He admitted that he suffered no injuries, nor was he obligated to comply with any conditions upon release and no medical treatment was received. Asked why, if he was suspected of supporting or being connected in any way to the LTTE, he would be released so quickly, and without any conditions, and the only explanation the claimant offered up was due to the fact that he answered all their questions. The Tribunal did not find the claimant credible that he was being persecuted, or that he was suspected of having ties to the LTTE and that he would only be detained so briefly. Given the powers bestowed upon the army and the police and their ability to detain people indefinitely if suspected of having LTTE affiliation, the Tribunal found the claimant's narrative and two alleged minor detentions to be implausible.

The Tribunal concedes that the National Documentation Package (NDP) is rife with support acknowledging the ill treatment of young Tamil males in Sri Lanka. The Tribunal also takes cognizance of the fact that the claimant is now in his thirties. The Tribunal further noted that notwithstanding the claimant's allegations, and alleged detentions on two occasions, he was never asked to comply with any conditions upon release. He was only told to leave the jurisdiction of XXXX. The Tribunal did not find the claimant credible that the police conditions upon his release would be to simply leave XXXX. The Tribunal found the testimony by the claimant regarding his detention and subsequent release to be suspect and not plausible.

By the claimant's own admission, he was a young Tamil male but had no serious problems before XXXX 2008. Even then, other than regular checking to which he testified, everyone was subjected to from time to time, he only identified his first problem at the age of 28 years old. According to his story, he lived in XXXX from 1997 to 2008 pretty much undisturbed. Asked to explain why then he would start to become a person of interest and accused of LTTE support or membership suddenly in 2008 and the claimant provided no explanation. Given the claimant's long standing presence in XXXX, the fact that he went to school and was gainfully employed by a Sinhalese, XXXX XXXX firm, never having had any problems up to the age of 28 (notwithstanding that he testified that two of his siblings left Sri Lanka in 1996 and 1998) the Tribunal found the claimant's story implausible.

Further, the Tribunal notes that the claimant is extremely well educated. By his testimony, he was continuously employed with seemingly no issues or problems finding or maintaining employment. The claimant submitted a letter from his former employer which he obtained on XXXX, 20093 even though he resigned on XXXX, 2008. He testified that he had to leave his job because it was too uncomfortable to work there as he was suspected of being an LTTE supporter or member. Asked why his alleged problems at work were not identified in his POE materials or PIF and the claimant failed to reply.

The claimant's oral testimony regarding the hardship he allegedly endured while working at XXXX was completely inconsistent with the reference letter4 he submitted to support his claim. The letter itself, which is a glowing recommendation letter for the claimant, indicated that the claimant left the company and was XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX). The letter refers to the claimant as hard working, honest and a good team player. It goes on at length to state that the claimant has good communication skills and took on challenging work. It further identifies the claimant as a pleasant young man who got on well with his colleagues and the management. The letter concludes stating that the claimant was a member of their XXXX XXXX and participated in the XXXX-XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX. The letter wishes the claimant all the best in his future endeavours. The Tribunal found that this letter, the only piece of evidence on behalf of the claimant's cause, is completely inconsistent with the claimant's allegations that he was being persecuted at work by everyone as they suspected him of being an LTTE member and that he had to resign as a result. This put the claimant's entire credibility into question.

Further impacting on the claimant's credibility was the fact that he mentioned that there is a sponsorship application pending in Canada, for a number of years now, for him and his family. Asked what the status was of that application and the claimant admitted that he had no knowledge of it and that he made no efforts to inquire as to timing or where his application was in the process. According to his testimony, after his second alleged detention, the one and only condition he was given was that he was told to leave XXXX and go back up north. He admitted that there were no death threats and nothing to indicate that if he left XXXX and headed up north as was suggested, that he would be pursued, by anyone, for any reason. Asked why he did not just relocate within Sri Lanka until the sponsorship application was complete but the claimant only stated that his father died and they had to resubmit the sponsorship forms.

The claimant was questioned about his alleged detention of five days on XXXX, 2009 and the Tribunal found that he was evasive, provided no details about what occurred, what was asked of him for five days, or where he was held exactly, and could not explain how or why he was released in such a short period. Again, when questioned about the incident of XXXX 2009, the claimant also had little or no information about how he was detained, where, why, or what differed from the first alleged incident. On this occasion he advised that upon payment of a bribe by his uncle, he was released within eight days. The Tribunal noted that the claimant indicated that the underlying premise of his detentions was due to his nationality (Tamil) and possible connection to the LTTE. The claimant was evasive and never directly responded to the question, nor satisfied the Tribunal as to why he was believed to be linked to the LTTE or why exactly he was detained for such a short time on each occasion. He was asked but failed to explain why, if his brother left in 1998, and his sister in 1996, he failed to join them until 2009. He was further asked but failed to explain why, if he was in the process of a sponsorship application through his sister, he would not just find an alternative location in Sri Lanka to await the process and come to Canada directly by legitimate ends. This also put his credibility into question and led the Tribunal to determine that based on his actions there was a lack of subjective fear.

Further still, notwithstanding that the claimant testified at the beginning of the hearing that his PIF contained all information and that it was up to date, at the end of the hearing, when asked if anyone has been looking for the claimant since his departure or if there is a warrant out for his arrest, he testified that his mother was approached by two men in XXXX 2010. These individuals were not known to his mother but they asked about the claimant. Asked why he failed to include this information as an amendment to his PIF and the claimant said it was a mistake. Asked if his mother had any proof of these individuals looking for the claimant, if there was a warrant for his arrest, or if his mother could describe them, or further if the claimant had asked his mother to provide an attestation letter to corroborate that people are looking for him and he admitted that she did not have any proof and that he failed to ask her to provide anything. Given the other credibility issues and the claimant's lack of corroborating evidence, the Tribunal found that the claimant was fabricating elements of his narrative and adding information as he went along to suggest that he is currently being sought after. The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant left in XXXX 2009 and that no one would contact his mother until XXXX 2010 to inquire as to his whereabouts. Asked for an explanation and the claimant said it was because his mother told people the claimant was in India. The Tribunal was not satisfied with this response as it did not make sense and failed to address why two years would go by before anyone looked for him.

Overall, the Tribunal did not find the claimant credible and did not believe that he was being sought after by anyone prior to his departure, nor in XXXX 2010, nor that he would be sought after were he to return to Sri Lanka. Asylum Forum Shopping - Delay in claiming

An additional negative inference impacting on the claimant's credibility was the fact that the claimant left Sri Lanka on XXXX, 2009, went to Russia, United Arab Emirates, Cuba, Panama, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic, allegedly in fear for his life, but did not claim for asylum in any of the eligible jurisdictions who are signatories to the Convention. He then reached the U.S. in XXXX 2009 and filed an asylum claim, which he later withdrew on XXXX, 2009, following which he came to Canada on XXXX, 2009 and claimed for refugee protection.

Asked why, he failed to claim elsewhere and would then risk withdrawing his application in the U.S. to file a separate claim in Canada, especially when he originally had a sponsorship application pending in Canada and/or when he was already in the asylum process in the U.S. and the claimant was non-responsive stating only that he did what the agent told him to do. Asked for a copy of his U.S. asylum claim document and what story he gave in the U.S. but the claimant said he did not have any of his U.S. materials. He failed to explain why not. Asked why he withdrew his claim in the U.S. and he indicated that it was what the agent instructed him, and two others that he was traveling with (and ended up being detained with in the U.S.), to do. Plus he testified that the judge told him to, so that he could come to Canada. He also added that it was because he has siblings in Canada and it was his intention to come here. Given the prior credibility issues in addition to the claimant's extensive travel from country to country for close to nine months (with a four month stay in the U.S.) and a voluntary withdrawal of his U.S. asylum claim, the Tribunal found that the claimant's actions were not consistent with those of someone in fear for his life. Section 96

In his POE and PIF materials the claimant mentions two detentions, one in 2008 and one in 2009. He admitted that he never suffered anything prior to 2008 and that he went to school and was thereafter gainfully employed in Sri Lanka, notwithstanding that his brother and sister had problems and left the country more than a decade before him. While the Tribunal acknowledges that the claimant is a Tamil male, by his own testimony he failed to establish that he was being persecuted, or that it was due to his race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or his political opinion.

Asked whom he feared in his PIF and POE notes, the claimant listed the police and the army. He was extremely vague and was not more specific than that. Asked if he had any problems prior to 2008 and he said he did not. Asked why he was detained on XXXX, 2008 and why only held for five days and released without any conditions, but the claimant could not say other than to testify that he and three others were taken off a bus and detained and that someone from his office came and managed to have him released. He then returned to work. The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant was seriously being considered a suspected LTTE supporter or member and that during this volatile period in Sri Lankan history, that the claimant would be released in less than five days and simply return to work.

The second incident allegedly occurred six months later on XXXX, 2009, several weeks after the claimant resigned from his job. On this occasion he was allegedly taken by a white van, while on his way to the library, by army people in green shirts. He could not say who was responsible for taking him but he mentioned that his assailants spoke in both Sinhalese and Tamil and in his materials identified the police as the ones who arrested him. He was again accused of helping the LTTE but failed to explain in what capacity he was suspected of having helped. On both occasions he testified that he was questioned extensively about his family and then released this second time, within eight days. Even if the Tribunal found that the claimant had been detained on two occasions, he did not credibly convince the Tribunal that he was being systematically persecuted, nor did the claimant credibly convey to the Tribunal that he would be subject to a serious possibility of being persecuted in the future for any reason, especially in light of the documentary evidence regarding the Government victory over the LTTE in May of 2009. 5 Given all of the above, the Tribunal finds that the claimant failed to meet the criteria for qualifying as a Convention refugee.

The Tribunal notes that, according to the NDP, this was a highly sensitive period in Sri Lanka's history and that the Sri Lankan army was in full force in addressing the 25-year war with the LTTE. Asked if he sustained any injuries during his alleged detentions, and the claimant said that he was hit with sticks. Asked what injuries he suffered but the claimant was extremely vague and failed to identify what or where his injuries supposedly were. Asked if he went for medical attention and he said he went to a private hospital. Asked which one and he failed to give the name. Asked what treatment he received and if he had any proof and he said he was given pain killers. Asked if he obtained a medical report and he admitted that he did not. Asked why not and his explanation was that he could not tell them that he was abducted or they would not give him medicine. The Tribunal found that the claimant did not make sense and seemed to be making things up as he went along. He then stated that they would tell him to go to the police, so he said nothing. The Tribunal found that information was not forthcoming and that the claimant failed to credibly establish that he sought any medical attention to the satisfaction of the Tribunal. He further failed to extend reasonable efforts to obtain any information to corroborate any of his allegations. The claimant testified that on each occasion, he was released, with no conditions. After the first incident he said he was told that they would be watching him and that his company would be accountable. After the second incident he was allegedly told to leave XXXX. The Tribunal also found the claimant's account of his alleged two releases highly suspect, especially in light of what was going on in Sri Lanka at the time.

The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant was detained on two separate occasions. Further, given his testimony that he lived in XXXX, undisturbed from 1997 to 2008, the claimant, by his own testimony, failed to support any finding of persecution. The Tribunal also noted that given the breadth of materials in the NDP, that the powers of the Sri Lankan government were such that they could hold a suspect indefinitely, and yet, the claimant was released within five or eight days on each occasion. As such, the Tribunal found that the claimant was not credible and that no systematic persecution for a Convention ground based on his race, religion or nationality for being a young, Tamil, Hindu, male, membership in a particular group or imputed political opinion was credibly established.

The claimant was asked if anyone has been looking for him and he testified that he knew of no one looking for him. Asked if his mother or brother have been contacted and at first he admitted that they had not been, but then mentioned two people approached his mother in XXXX 2010. As this incident was found not to be credible, the Tribunal does not believe that anyone was, is or would be looking for the claimant. Section 97(1)

The Tribunal then considered whether the claimant's removal would subject him personally to the dangers and risks stipulated in Section 97(1). The Federal Court has held that, pursuant to IRPA section 97(1): (i) there must be persuasive evidence (i.e., balance of probabilities) establishing the facts on which a claimant relies. This is to say that the claimant faces a danger or risk of being tortured, risk to life, risk of harm or of having cruel and unusual treatment, or punishment, inflicted upon the claimant's return.6 Section 97(1)(a)

In light of the changes in Sri Lanka7 and the absence of credible evidence to suggest he would face any danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the "Convention Against Torture", the Tribunal finds that this ground is not open to the claimant. Section 97(1)(b)

The Tribunal then considered whether the claimant is a person who faces a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Given that no reasons, other than those analyzed under Section 96 above were presented to the Tribunal, the Tribunal finds that this ground is not open to the claimant. As such, he is not a person in need of protection.

Notwithstanding the various credibility issues raised, the claimant's profile and given the change in circumstances in the political environment in Sri Lanka today8, the Tribunal does not believe that it is more likely than not that the claimant would be targeted were he to return to Sri Lanka. Given that the Tribunal does not believe that anyone has been looking for him, the Tribunal was not convinced that were the claimant to return to Sri Lanka, he would be of interest to the Sri Lankan authorities. The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant is being sought after in his country nor that he would be were he to return to Sri Lanka.

Upon raising the issue of a change in circumstances in Sri Lanka in light of the LTTE defeat by the Sri Lankan army in May 20099, it may be argued that compelling reasons should be considered. The Tribunal draws reference to the persuasive decision VA9-0216610 which details the historical events that give rise to a change of circumstances in Sri Lanka. Given this change of circumstances, as documented in the jurisprudence and the NDP, the Tribunal considered whether the claimant's alleged experiences constituted atrocious treatment. Taking into consideration the claimant's age, cultural background and social experiences, the Tribunal found that the claimant's case did not merit a finding of compelling reasons as his alleged encounters were brief, unsubstantiated, not deemed systematic in nature and overall, found not to be credible. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

In order to determine if there is an IFA, the test to be applied is: (i) if there is another part of the country, where the claimant would not have a well-founded fear of persecution and (ii) that it would not be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to this location.

By the claimant's own testimony, his mother and brother continue to reside in Sri Lanka and have had no problems. Further he testified that the conditions of his release in XXXX 2009 were allegedly that he leave XXXX and go to the north. During the hearing the claimant was asked if he could relocate to Kandy or Jaffna. He did not refute the ability to find a place to live or to obtain work. His only concern was that he would have to register, so the authorities would be able to easily locate him. The claimant was asked if he was aware of any warrant for his arrest and he admitted that he was not aware of anything. Having not credibly convinced the Tribunal that the authorities or anyone else is looking for the claimant, or that there was a warrant for his arrest pending, and given that the recent documentation pertaining to the situation in Sri Lanka suggests that registration requirements are being eased in a number of locations,11 the Tribunal found that the claimant did not establish that he could not easily relocate to Kandy or Jaffna. Given the above factors and the claimant's education and skill set, the Tribunal did not believe that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to either of these locations.

Based on the totality of the evidence before it, the Tribunal finds there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted for a section 96 Convention ground, if he was to return to Sri Lanka. Nor does the Tribunal find the claimant to be a person in need of protection under section 97 (1)(a) nor section 97(1)(b). As such, he is not a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection.

For all of the reasons cited above, the Tribunal rejects the claim for refugee protection.
